# Unit 1: Limits and Continuity

## Overview
This unit introduces the foundational ideas of **limits** and **continuity**, which underlie nearly every major topic in AP Calculus BC, including **derivatives**, **integrals**, and **series**. On the AP exam, students must evaluate limits algebraically, graphically, numerically, and analytically, including limits involving **indeterminate forms** and the use of **L'Hôpital's Rule**.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Limit** | The value that $$f(x)$$ approaches as $$x$$ approaches a given number or infinity. | Limits are the gateway to derivatives and integrals and are tested in multiple representations. |
| **One-Sided Limits** | Limits from the left or right only: $$\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)$$ and $$\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$$. | AP questions often ask whether a two-sided limit exists by comparing one-sided limits. |
| **Infinite Limits** | Limits where $$f(x)$$ grows without bound as $$x \to a$$. | Used to identify **vertical asymptotes** and behavior near discontinuities. |
| **Limits at Infinity** | Behavior of $$f(x)$$ as $$x \to \infty$$ or $$x \to -\infty$$. | Important for identifying **horizontal asymptotes** and end behavior. |
| **Continuity** | A function is continuous at $$x=a$$ if the limit exists, the function value exists, and they are equal. | AP problems frequently ask students to justify continuity or identify discontinuities. |
| **Types of Discontinuities** | Removable, jump, and infinite discontinuities. | Students must recognize and classify discontinuities from graphs, equations, or tables. |
| **Indeterminate Forms** | Expressions such as $$\frac{0}{0}$$ or $$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$ that require further analysis. | Common on FRQs and MCQs; students must know when simplification or L'Hôpital's Rule applies. |
| **L'Hôpital's Rule** | A method for evaluating certain indeterminate limits by differentiating numerator and denominator. | Frequently tested in BC for more advanced limit evaluation, especially with transcendental functions. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Identify the limit expression] --> B{Direct substitution works?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Evaluate the limit directly]
    B -->|No| D{Indeterminate form?}
    D -->|No| E[Analyze graphically or by known behavior]
    D -->|Yes| F[Rewrite algebraically]
    F --> G[Factor, rationalize, combine, or use identities]
    G --> H{Indeterminate form remains?}
    H -->|No| I[Evaluate simplified limit]
    H -->|Yes| J{Form is "$$\frac{0}{0}$$" or "$$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$"?}
    J -->|Yes| K[Apply L'Hôpital's Rule]
    K --> L[Differentiate top and bottom]
    L --> M{Limit now evaluable?}
    M -->|Yes| N[State final limit]
    M -->|No| O[Repeat if still indeterminate]
    J -->|No| P[Rewrite into a usable form first]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Definition** | **Expression** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|---|
| **Limit Definition** | $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$$ | As $$x$$ gets arbitrarily close to $$a$$, $$f(x)$$ gets arbitrarily close to $$L$$. |
| **Two-Sided Limit Exists** | $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \iff \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)=L \text{ and } \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)=L$$ | Both one-sided limits must exist and be equal. |
| **Continuity at a Point** | $$f \text{ is continuous at } a \iff \lim_{x \to a} f(x)=f(a)$$ | Equivalent to: function exists, limit exists, and they are equal. |
| **Limit Laws** | $$\lim_{x \to a}[f(x)\pm g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a}f(x)\pm \lim_{x \to a}g(x)$$ | Limits distribute across sums and differences when both limits exist. |
|  | $$\lim_{x \to a}[f(x)g(x)] = \left(\lim_{x \to a}f(x)\right)\left(\lim_{x \to a}g(x)\right)$$ | Product law. |
|  | $$\lim_{x \to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{\lim_{x \to a}f(x)}{\lim_{x \to a}g(x)} \quad \text{if } \lim_{x \to a}g(x)\ne 0$$ | Quotient law. |
| **Squeeze Theorem** | If $$g(x)\le f(x)\le h(x)$$ and $$\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=\lim_{x\to a}h(x)=L$$, then $$\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$$ | Useful when direct evaluation is difficult. |
| **L'Hôpital's Rule** | If $$\lim_{x \to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$$ gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$ or $$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$, then $$\lim_{x \to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\lim_{x \to a}\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$$, if the latter limit exists. | Only applies to specific indeterminate quotient forms. |
| **Common Indeterminate Forms** | $$\frac{0}{0}, \frac{\infty}{\infty}, 0\cdot\infty, \infty-\infty, 1^\infty, 0^0, \infty^0$$ | These forms do **not** determine the limit by themselves. |
| **Continuity of Common Functions** | Polynomials, exponentials, trig functions, and rational functions are continuous on their domains. | Helps justify continuity quickly on AP free-response questions. |

### Especially Important Standard Limits
- $$\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1$$
- $$\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x}=0$$
- $$\lim_{x \to \infty}\frac{1}{x}=0$$

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept** | **Definition / Behavior** | **How to Recognize** | **AP-Relevant Difference** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Removable Discontinuity** | Limit exists, but $$f(a)$$ is missing or not equal to the limit. | A “hole” in the graph; often caused by a factor that cancels. | Can often be fixed by redefining the function at one point. |
| **Jump Discontinuity** | Left- and right-hand limits exist but are not equal. | A sudden step in the graph. | Two-sided limit does **not** exist. |
| **Infinite Discontinuity** | Function grows without bound near a point. | Vertical asymptote. | Often described using infinite limits. |
| **Continuous Function** | No break at the point; limit equals function value. | Graph can be drawn through the point without interruption. | Supports use of direct substitution and many later theorems. |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **undefined** with **does not exist**: a function value may be undefined at $$x=a$$ while the limit still exists.
- Using **L'Hôpital's Rule** on expressions that are not first rewritten into $$\frac{0}{0}$$ or $$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$ form.
- Forgetting that a two-sided limit exists **only if** the left- and right-hand limits are equal.
- Canceling factors without noting the original function may still be undefined at the canceled value, creating a **removable discontinuity**.
- Assuming continuity everywhere for rational functions; they are only continuous where the denominator is nonzero.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can explain what a **limit** represents numerically, graphically, and algebraically.
- [ ] I can determine whether a two-sided limit exists by comparing **one-sided limits**.
- [ ] I can evaluate limits using **direct substitution**, factoring, rationalizing, or identities.
- [ ] I can identify and classify **removable**, **jump**, and **infinite discontinuities**.
- [ ] I can state the three conditions required for **continuity at a point**.
- [ ] I can analyze **limits at infinity** and identify horizontal or vertical asymptotic behavior.
- [ ] I can recognize **indeterminate forms** and decide whether algebraic rewriting or **L'Hôpital's Rule** is appropriate.
- [ ] I can justify answers using proper AP Calculus language, including notation such as $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$$ and continuity statements.

units.note:
# Unit 2: Differentiation: Definition and Fundamental Properties

## Overview
This unit introduces the **derivative** as a limit that measures **instantaneous rate of change** and the **slope of a tangent line**. You will learn how to compute derivatives using the definition and the main differentiation rules, then apply them to **linear approximation**—all of which are foundational skills that appear frequently in both multiple-choice and free-response AP Calculus BC questions.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Derivative as a limit** | The derivative of $$f$$ at $$x=a$$ is defined by a limit of a difference quotient. | AP questions often test whether you can interpret or evaluate a derivative directly from its definition. |
| **Difference quotient** | The expression $$\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$ or $$\dfrac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}$$ before taking the limit. | You must recognize it in algebraic form and simplify it correctly. |
| **Tangent line slope** | $$f'(a)$$ gives the slope of the tangent line to $$y=f(x)$$ at $$x=a$$. | AP problems connect derivatives to graph interpretation and tangent line equations. |
| **Instantaneous rate of change** | The derivative describes how fast a quantity changes at a specific input value. | Frequently used in context-based word problems involving motion, growth, or related quantities. |
| **Basic differentiation rules** | Constant, power, constant multiple, sum, and difference rules. | These are the computational backbone of nearly every derivative problem on the exam. |
| **Product, quotient, and chain rules** | Rules for differentiating products, quotients, and compositions of functions. | AP BC expects fluent rule selection and accurate execution, especially in multi-step expressions. |
| **Higher-order derivatives** | Derivatives of derivatives, such as $$f''(x)$$. | Important for interpreting velocity/acceleration and graph behavior later in the course. |
| **Linear approximation** | Using the tangent line near $$x=a$$ to estimate $$f(x)$$. | A classic AP application that connects local linearity, tangent lines, and estimation. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Start with a function $$f(x)$$"] --> B["Form the difference quotient $$\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$"]
    B --> C["Take the limit as $$h \to 0$$"]
    C --> D["Obtain the derivative $$f'(x)$$"]
    D --> E["Interpret as slope of tangent line"]
    D --> F["Interpret as instantaneous rate of change"]
    D --> G["Use differentiation rules to compute efficiently"]
    G --> H["Evaluate at a point $$x=a$$ if needed"]
    H --> I["Build tangent line or linear approximation"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Idea** | **Formula** |
|---|---|
| **Derivative definition** | $$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$$ |
| **Equivalent point-based definition** | $$f'(a)=\lim_{x\to a}\dfrac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}$$ |
| **Derivative as tangent slope** | $$m_{\text{tan}}=f'(a)$$ |
| **Tangent line equation** | $$y-f(a)=f'(a)(x-a)$$ |
| **Constant rule** | $$\dfrac{d}{dx}[c]=0$$ |
| **Power rule** | $$\dfrac{d}{dx}[x^n]=nx^{n-1}$$ |
| **Constant multiple rule** | $$\dfrac{d}{dx}[cf(x)]=c f'(x)$$ |
| **Sum rule** | $$\dfrac{d}{dx}[f(x)+g(x)]=f'(x)+g'(x)$$ |
| **Difference rule** | $$\dfrac{d}{dx}[f(x)-g(x)]=f'(x)-g'(x)$$ |
| **Product rule** | $$\dfrac{d}{dx}[f(x)g(x)]=f'(x)g(x)+f(x)g'(x)$$ |
| **Quotient rule** | $$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right]=\dfrac{f'(x)g(x)-f(x)g'(x)}{[g(x)]^2}$$ |
| **Chain rule** | $$\dfrac{d}{dx}[f(g(x))]=f'(g(x))g'(x)$$ |
| **Higher-order derivative** | $$f''(x)=\dfrac{d}{dx}[f'(x)]$$ |
| **Linearization at $$x=a$$** | $$L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$$ |
| **Approximation near $$x=a$$** | $$f(x)\approx L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$$ |

### Must-know interpretations
- **If** $$f'(a)>0$$, then $$f$$ is increasing at that point.
- **If** $$f'(a)<0$$, then $$f$$ is decreasing at that point.
- **If** $$f'(a)=0$$, the tangent line is horizontal, but that does **not** automatically mean a maximum or minimum.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection / Difference** | **AP Significance** |
|---|---|---|
| **Average rate of change** vs. **instantaneous rate of change** | Average rate uses a secant slope over an interval: $$\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$$. Instantaneous rate uses a tangent slope at one point: $$f'(a)$$. | AP often asks you to move from secant slope to tangent slope through a limit. |
| **Derivative from definition** vs. **derivative from rules** | The definition explains what the derivative means; rules make computation fast. | You may be required to justify a derivative from first principles or compute efficiently using rules. |
| **Tangent line** vs. **linear approximation** | The tangent line is the exact line touching the curve at $$x=a$$; linear approximation uses that line to estimate nearby values. | AP questions often ask for both the tangent line equation and an estimate of a function value near $$a$$. |
| **First derivative** vs. **second derivative** | $$f'(x)$$ measures rate of change of $$f$$; $$f''(x)$$ measures rate of change of the rate of change. | Essential for interpreting motion and later graph analysis. |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Forgetting that the **derivative definition** requires a **limit**; the difference quotient alone is **not** the derivative.
- Using the **power rule** incorrectly on composite functions, such as differentiating $$[g(x)]^n$$ without also multiplying by $$g'(x)$$.
- Mixing up the **product rule** and **quotient rule**, especially forgetting that the denominator in the quotient rule is $$[g(x)]^2$$.
- Assuming that if $$f'(a)=0$$, then $$f$$ must have a local extremum at $$x=a$$. A horizontal tangent does not guarantee a max or min.
- Using **linear approximation** too far from the base point $$x=a$$; it is only reliable **near** the point of tangency.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can state the **definition of the derivative** using a limit.
- [ ] I can interpret $$f'(a)$$ as both a **tangent line slope** and an **instantaneous rate of change**.
- [ ] I can compute a derivative from the **difference quotient** by simplifying and taking a limit.
- [ ] I can apply the **power, sum, difference, and constant multiple rules** correctly.
- [ ] I can use the **product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule** on more complicated expressions.
- [ ] I can find the equation of a **tangent line** at a given point.
- [ ] I can write and use a **linearization** $$L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$$ to estimate nearby values.
- [ ] I can distinguish **average rate of change** from **instantaneous rate of change** and explain how limits connect them.

A rule stating that for real $$n$$, the derivative of $$x^n$$ is $$nx^{n-1}$$, wherever the expression is defined.

# Unit 3: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions

## Overview
This unit develops three major differentiation tools: the **chain rule** for composite functions, **implicit differentiation** for equations that do not explicitly solve for $$y$$, and derivatives of **inverse functions**. These ideas are heavily tested on the AP Calculus BC exam because they connect algebraic structure to derivative reasoning and appear in both procedural and conceptual free-response and multiple-choice questions.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Composite functions** | A function built from one function inside another, such as $$f(g(x))$$ | AP questions often require identifying nested structure before differentiating |
| **Chain rule** | The derivative rule for compositions: differentiate the outside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside | One of the most frequently used differentiation rules on the exam |
| **Repeated chain rule** | Applying the chain rule more than once when a function has multiple layers | Common in BC problems with powers, trig, exponentials, and radicals combined |
| **Implicit differentiation** | Differentiating both sides of an equation involving $$x$$ and $$y$$, treating $$y$$ as a function of $$x$$ | Essential for finding $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ when equations are not solved for $$y$$ |
| **Related use of $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ in implicit forms** | Solving for slope, tangent lines, or second derivatives from implicit equations | AP free-response often asks for slope at a point or where tangent lines are horizontal/vertical |
| **Inverse functions** | Functions that reverse each other, so that $$f^{-1}(f(x))=x$$ | Understanding inverses supports derivative formulas and graph interpretation |
| **Derivative of an inverse function** | A rule connecting the derivative of $$f^{-1}$$ to the derivative of $$f$$ | Frequently tested conceptually, especially with tables and function values |
| **Inverse trig derivatives** | Derivatives of functions like $$\sin^{-1}(x)$$ and $$\tan^{-1}(x)$$ | BC students must know these formulas and use them accurately in context |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Identify function structure] --> B{Explicit or implicit?}
    B -->|Explicit composite| C[Locate outer and inner functions]
    C --> D[Differentiate outer function]
    D --> E[Multiply by derivative of inner function]
    E --> F[Simplify carefully]

    B -->|Implicit relation| G[Differentiatie both sides with respect to x]
    G --> H["Apply chain rule to terms with y (include dy/dx)"]
    H --> I[Solve algebraically for dy/dx]
    I --> J[Evaluate at given point if needed]

    B -->|Inverse function question| K[Use inverse relationship]
    K --> L["Apply formula for derivative of inverse"]
    L --> M[Substitute known function value and derivative]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Idea** | **Formula** |
|---|---|
| **Chain rule** | $$\frac{d}{dx}\left[f(g(x))\right]=f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)$$ |
| **Power form of chain rule** | $$\frac{d}{dx}\left[(u(x))^n\right]=n(u(x))^{n-1}u'(x)$$ |
| **General implicit differentiation idea** | If $$F(x,y)=0$$, then differentiate both sides with respect to $$x$$, treating $$y$$ as $$y(x)$$ |
| **Derivative of $$y^n$$ in implicit form** | $$\frac{d}{dx}\left[y^n\right]=ny^{n-1}\frac{dy}{dx}$$ |
| **Product with implicit variable** | $$\frac{d}{dx}\left[x\,y\right]=x\frac{dy}{dx}+y$$ |
| **Derivative of an inverse function** | $$\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)=\frac{1}{f'\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)}$$ |
| **Equivalent inverse derivative form** | If $$y=f^{-1}(x)$$, then $$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{f'(y)}$$ |
| **Inverse relationship identity** | $$f\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=x \quad \text{and} \quad f^{-1}(f(x))=x$$ |
| **Derivative of $$\sin^{-1}(x)$$** | $$\frac{d}{dx}\left[\sin^{-1}(x)\right]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \quad \text{for } |x|<1$$ |
| **Derivative of $$\cos^{-1}(x)$$** | $$\frac{d}{dx}\left[\cos^{-1}(x)\right]=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \quad \text{for } |x|<1$$ |
| **Derivative of $$\tan^{-1}(x)$$** | $$\frac{d}{dx}\left[\tan^{-1}(x)\right]=\frac{1}{1+x^2}$$ |

### High-value reminders
- For **implicit differentiation**, every time you differentiate a term containing $$y$$, multiply by $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ when required by the chain rule.
- For **inverse derivatives**, you usually need:
  $$f(a)=b \Rightarrow f^{-1}(b)=a$$
  so table questions often require finding the matching input-output pair first.
- A function must be **one-to-one** on the relevant interval to have an inverse function.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection** | **Key Difference** | **Typical AP Use** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ordinary differentiation vs. chain rule** | Both find derivatives | The chain rule is needed when one function is inside another | Recognizing when simple rules are not enough |
| **Explicit vs. implicit differentiation** | Both produce $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ | Explicit functions are solved for $$y$$; implicit relations are not | Finding slopes from equations like $$x^2+y^2=25$$ |
| **Chain rule vs. inverse derivative formula** | Both rely on composition | The inverse formula comes from differentiating $$f(f^{-1}(x))=x$$ | Conceptual problems connecting function and inverse |
| **Inverse trig functions vs. reciprocal trig functions** | Names look similar | $$\sin^{-1}(x)$$ means inverse sine, not $$\frac{1}{\sin(x)}$$ | A classic notation trap on AP questions |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Forgetting the extra factor of $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ when differentiating terms involving $$y$$ implicitly, such as writing $$\frac{d}{dx}[y^3]=3y^2$$ instead of $$3y^2\frac{dy}{dx}$$.
- Using the **chain rule** incompletely by differentiating the outside function but not multiplying by the derivative of the inside.
- Confusing **inverse trig notation** with reciprocal trig notation: $$\sin^{-1}(x)\neq \csc(x)$$.
- Using the inverse derivative formula without first finding the correct corresponding input, such as failing to convert from $$f(a)=b$$ to $$f^{-1}(b)=a$$.
- Solving an implicit derivative correctly but not substituting the given point to find the numerical slope or tangent line.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can identify when a function is a **composite function** and choose the **chain rule**.
- [ ] I can differentiate multistep compositions such as powers of trig, exponential, or radical expressions.
- [ ] I can perform **implicit differentiation** on equations involving both $$x$$ and $$y$$.
- [ ] I can solve algebraically for $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ after differentiating implicitly.
- [ ] I can find the slope of a tangent line to a curve defined implicitly at a specific point.
- [ ] I can use $$\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x)=\frac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}$$ correctly.
- [ ] I can interpret inverse-function questions from equations, graphs, or tables.
- [ ] I can distinguish **inverse trig functions** from **reciprocal trig functions** and use the correct derivative formulas.

The process of differentiating an expression formed by substituting one function into another, often requiring identification of inner and outer parts before applying $$\frac{d}{dx}[f(g(x))]$$ appropriately.

# Unit 4: Contextual Applications of Differentiation

## Overview
This unit applies **derivatives** to real-world situations: interpreting **rates of change**, solving **related rates** problems, and analyzing **motion** using position, velocity, and acceleration. These ideas matter on the AP Exam because students must move beyond computing derivatives and use them to **model, interpret, and justify** behavior in context, often with units and sign analysis.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Rate of change in context** | Interpreting a derivative as how one quantity changes with respect to another | AP questions often ask for the meaning of $$f'(x)$$, including **units** and what positive/negative values imply |
| **Units of a derivative** | The units of $$\dfrac{dy}{dx}$$ are “units of $$y$$ per unit of $$x$$” | Students must explain derivative values in context, not just compute them |
| **Related rates** | Problems where multiple changing quantities are connected by an equation and differentiated with respect to time | A classic FRQ topic requiring setup, implicit differentiation, and substitution at the correct instant |
| **Implicit differentiation in applications** | Differentiating equations that define relationships indirectly | Essential in related rates when variables like $$r$$, $$h$$, $$x$$, and $$y$$ all depend on time |
| **Position, velocity, and acceleration** | Motion relationships where velocity is the derivative of position and acceleration is the derivative of velocity | Central to interpreting motion graphs, finding speed, and determining when an object moves left/right or speeds up/slows down |
| **Average vs. instantaneous rate of change** | Average rate uses a secant slope; instantaneous rate uses a tangent slope | AP problems may ask students to compare numerical average change with derivative-based instantaneous change |
| **Speed vs. velocity** | Velocity includes direction; speed is the magnitude of velocity | A frequent source of mistakes, especially when velocity is negative |
| **Particle motion analysis** | Using signs of $$v(t)$$ and $$a(t)$$ to describe movement and changes in motion | Appears often in FRQs and MCQs involving tables, graphs, or formulas |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Identify the quantities that change] --> B[Define variables with units]
    B --> C[Write an equation relating the variables]
    C --> D[Differentiatie with respect to time]
    D --> E[Substitute the given values at the instant]
    E --> F[Solve for the unknown rate]
    F --> G[Interpret the sign and include units]
```

### Motion-analysis workflow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Position function $$s(t)$$] --> B[Differentiate to get velocity $$v(t)=s'(t)$$]
    B --> C[Differentiate to get acceleration $$a(t)=v'(t)=s''(t)$$]
    B --> D[Use sign of $$v(t)$$ to determine direction of motion]
    C --> E[Combine signs of $$v(t)$$ and $$a(t)$$ to determine speeding up or slowing down]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Idea** | **Formula / Rule** |
|---|---|
| **Average rate of change** | $$\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$$ |
| **Instantaneous rate of change** | $$f'(a)=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$$ |
| **Derivative as a rate** | If $$y=f(x)$$, then $$\dfrac{dy}{dx}$$ measures the rate at which $$y$$ changes with respect to $$x$$ |
| **Units of a derivative** | $$\dfrac{\text{units of output}}{\text{units of input}}$$ |
| **Related rates principle** | If variables depend on time, differentiate both sides of the relationship with respect to $$t$$ |
| **Chain rule in related rates** | $$\dfrac{d}{dt}[x^n]=nx^{n-1}\dfrac{dx}{dt}$$ |
| **Velocity** | $$v(t)=s'(t)$$ |
| **Acceleration** | $$a(t)=v'(t)=s''(t)$$ |
| **Speed** | $$\text{speed}=|v(t)|$$ |
| **Total distance traveled** | Over an interval, total distance is found by accumulating the magnitude of velocity; if using integrals later, this becomes $$\int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt$$ |
| **Moving right / left** | Moving right when $$v(t)>0$$; moving left when $$v(t)<0$$ |
| **Speeding up / slowing down** | An object is **speeding up** when $$v(t)$$ and $$a(t)$$ have the same sign, and **slowing down** when they have opposite signs |

### Common related-rates equations
Students should recognize common geometric models:

- **Circle area**: $$A=\pi r^2$$
- **Sphere volume**: $$V=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$
- **Cone volume**: $$V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$$
- **Pythagorean relationship**: $$x^2+y^2=z^2$$

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection** | **Key Difference** | **Typical AP Use** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Average rate of change** vs. **instantaneous rate of change** | Both describe how a quantity changes | Average uses two points; instantaneous uses the derivative at one point | Comparing secant slope to tangent slope |
| **Velocity** vs. **speed** | Both describe motion | Velocity can be negative; speed is always nonnegative: $$|v(t)|$$ | Interpreting direction versus magnitude |
| **Position** vs. **displacement** vs. **distance traveled** | All involve motion over time | Displacement is net change in position; distance traveled accounts for all movement | AP often asks for verbal interpretation from graphs or tables |
| **Related rates setup** vs. **solving the rate** | Both are part of one problem | Setup requires the correct equation before substitution; solving comes after differentiation | Many students lose points by substituting too early |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **velocity** with **speed**. If $$v(t)=-3$$, the velocity is negative, but the speed is $$3$$.
- Substituting numerical values into a **related rates** equation **before differentiating**. Differentiate the general relationship first.
- Forgetting that all changing quantities in related rates are functions of time, so terms like $$r^2$$ become $$2r\dfrac{dr}{dt}$$ when differentiated.
- Ignoring **units** in contextual questions. A derivative answer without units or interpretation is often incomplete.
- Misidentifying **speeding up** and **slowing down**. The sign of $$a(t)$$ alone is not enough; compare the signs of $$v(t)$$ and $$a(t)$$ together.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] I can interpret **$$f'(x)$$** as an instantaneous rate of change in words and with correct units.
- [ ] I can distinguish between **average rate of change** and **instantaneous rate of change**.
- [ ] I can set up a **related rates** problem by defining variables and writing an equation relating them.
- [ ] I can use **implicit differentiation** with respect to time to find an unknown rate.
- [ ] I can identify when to use geometric formulas such as $$A=\pi r^2$$ or $$V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$$ in a related-rates context.
- [ ] I can find **velocity** and **acceleration** from a position function $$s(t)$$.
- [ ] I can determine when an object is moving left/right and speeding up/slowing down using the signs of $$v(t)$$ and $$a(t)$$.
- [ ] I can explain the difference among **position**, **displacement**, **velocity**, **speed**, and **distance traveled** in context.

--- 

### Final tip
In this unit, AP success depends on more than calculation: always **name the quantity**, **state the units**, and **interpret the sign** of your answer in context.

# Unit 5: Analytical Applications of Differentiation

## Overview
This unit uses the **derivative** to analyze how functions behave: where they increase or decrease, where they have **extreme values**, how they curve, and how to solve **optimization** problems. These ideas are heavily tested on the AP Calculus BC exam in both multiple-choice and free-response settings, especially when you must justify conclusions using the **Mean Value Theorem**, sign analysis, and derivative-based reasoning.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Critical points** | Values of $$x$$ where $$f'(x)=0$$ or $$f'(x)$$ does not exist | Used to locate candidates for local and absolute extrema |
| **Mean Value Theorem (MVT)** | If $$f$$ is continuous on $$[a,b]$$ and differentiable on $$(a,b)$$, then some $$c \in (a,b)$$ satisfies $$f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$$ | Frequently tested as a theorem statement, condition check, or interpretation of average vs. instantaneous rate of change |
| **Increasing / decreasing behavior** | Determined by the sign of $$f'(x)$$ | Central to graph analysis and justification of local extrema |
| **First Derivative Test** | Uses sign changes in $$f'(x)$$ around critical points | Helps classify **local maxima** and **local minima** |
| **Concavity** | Determined by the sign of $$f''(x)$$ | Used to describe graph shape and support sketching |
| **Inflection points** | Points where concavity changes | AP questions often require distinguishing between $$f''(x)=0$$ and an actual change in concavity |
| **Second Derivative Test** | Uses $$f''(c)$$ to classify a critical point when $$f'(c)=0$$ | Efficient tool, but only valid under the right conditions |
| **Optimization** | Finding maximum or minimum values in applied contexts | A classic AP FRQ topic requiring modeling, domain restrictions, calculus work, and interpretation |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start with function or context] --> B[Find domain and any constraints]
    B --> C[Compute first derivative]
    C --> D[Find critical points where $$f'(x)=0$$ or undefined]
    D --> E[Make sign chart for $$f'(x)$$]
    E --> F[Determine increasing/decreasing intervals]
    F --> G[Classify local extrema with First Derivative Test]
    G --> H[Compute second derivative]
    H --> I[Analyze concavity using sign of $$f''(x)$$]
    I --> J[Identify possible inflection points]
    J --> K["If absolute extrema are needed, evaluate endpoints and critical points"]
    K --> L["If applied problem, interpret result in context with units"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Idea** | **Must Know Statement** |
|---|---|
| **Mean Value Theorem** | If $$f$$ is continuous on $$[a,b]$$ and differentiable on $$(a,b)$$, then there exists at least one $$c \in (a,b)$$ such that $$f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$$ |
| **Critical point definition** | A **critical point** occurs at $$x=c$$ if $$f'(c)=0$$ or $$f'(c)$$ does not exist, provided $$f(c)$$ exists |
| **Increasing / decreasing test** | If $$f'(x)>0$$ on an interval, then $$f$$ is increasing there; if $$f'(x)<0$$, then $$f$$ is decreasing there |
| **First Derivative Test** | If $$f'(x)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$c$$, then $$f(c)$$ is a local maximum; if negative to positive, then $$f(c)$$ is a local minimum |
| **Concavity test** | If $$f''(x)>0$$ on an interval, then $$f$$ is concave up; if $$f''(x)<0$$, then $$f$$ is concave down |
| **Inflection point condition** | A point is an inflection point only if the concavity changes there; having $$f''(x)=0$$ is not enough by itself |
| **Second Derivative Test** | If $$f'(c)=0$$ and $$f''(c)>0$$, then $$f(c)$$ is a local minimum; if $$f''(c)<0$$, then $$f(c)$$ is a local maximum; if $$f''(c)=0$$, the test is inconclusive |
| **Absolute Extreme Value strategy** | On a closed interval $$[a,b]$$, evaluate $$f(x)$$ at all critical points in $$(a,b)$$ and at endpoints $$a$$ and $$b$$; compare values |
| **Optimization setup** | Write an objective function $$Q(x)$$, use constraints to express it in one variable, find critical points in the feasible domain, then test candidates and interpret |

### Common derivative-based conclusions
- **Horizontal tangent:** $$f'(x)=0$$
- **Possible local extremum:** critical point of $$f$$
- **Possible inflection point:** where $$f''(x)=0$$ or undefined, followed by a concavity check

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection** | **Key Difference** |
|---|---|---|
| **Average rate of change** vs. **instantaneous rate of change** | Both describe how a quantity changes | Average rate uses $$\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$$ over an interval; instantaneous rate uses $$f'(x)$$ at one point |
| **Critical point** vs. **extremum** | Extrema often occur at critical points | Not every critical point is a max or min |
| **Concavity change** vs. **$$f''(x)=0$$** | Many inflection points occur where $$f''(x)=0$$ | But $$f''(x)=0$$ alone does not prove an inflection point |
| **Local extrema** vs. **absolute extrema** | Both describe highest/lowest behavior | Local compares nearby points; absolute compares all points in the domain or interval |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Derivative $$f'(x)$$] --> B[Sign of $$f'(x)$$]
    B --> C[Increasing or decreasing]
    C --> D[Local extrema]

    A2[Second derivative $$f''(x)$$] --> E[Sign of $$f''(x)$$]
    E --> F[Concavity]
    F --> G[Inflection behavior]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Forgetting to verify the **hypotheses** of the **Mean Value Theorem**: **continuity** on $$[a,b]$$ and **differentiability** on $$(a,b)$$ must be stated.
- Assuming that if $$f'(c)=0$$, then $$f(c)$$ must be a local max or min. A critical point may be neither.
- Claiming an **inflection point** just because $$f''(x)=0$$. You must show that concavity actually changes.
- Using the **Second Derivative Test** when $$f'(c)\neq 0$$ or treating $$f''(c)=0$$ as proof of anything definite.
- In optimization, finding a critical point but ignoring the **domain**, **endpoints**, or real-world constraints.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can correctly state the **Mean Value Theorem** and check whether its conditions are satisfied.
- [ ] I can find **critical points** by solving $$f'(x)=0$$ and identifying where $$f'(x)$$ is undefined.
- [ ] I can use a **sign chart** for $$f'(x)$$ to determine where a function is increasing or decreasing.
- [ ] I can classify **local maxima** and **local minima** using the **First Derivative Test**.
- [ ] I can use $$f''(x)$$ to determine **concavity** and identify actual **inflection points**.
- [ ] I can use the **Second Derivative Test** when appropriate and recognize when it is inconclusive.
- [ ] I can find **absolute extrema** on a closed interval by checking critical points and endpoints.
- [ ] I can set up and solve an **optimization** problem, then interpret the answer with correct context and units.

# Unit 6: Integration and Accumulation of Change

## Overview
This unit develops **integration** as the reverse of differentiation and as a tool for measuring **accumulated change**. You will connect **Riemann sums**, **definite integrals**, the **Fundamental Theorem of Calculus**, and advanced techniques like **integration by parts**, **partial fractions**, and **improper integrals**.

On the AP Calculus BC exam, this unit is central because it blends **conceptual understanding**, **graphical interpretation**, and **symbolic computation**. Many free-response and multiple-choice questions test both how to evaluate integrals and how to interpret them in context.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Riemann Sum** | A finite sum that approximates the area under a curve using rectangles. | AP questions often ask for interpretation, setup, and comparison of left, right, and midpoint sums. |
| **Definite Integral** | The limit of Riemann sums, representing **net signed area** or accumulated change. | You must interpret integrals in context and connect them to motion, area, and accumulation. |
| **Antiderivative** | A function $$F(x)$$ such that $$F'(x)=f(x)$$. | Essential for evaluating integrals and solving differential equations. |
| **Fundamental Theorem of Calculus** | Connects differentiation and integration in two major ways. | One of the most tested ideas in BC: evaluate integrals and differentiate accumulation functions. |
| **Accumulation Function** | A function defined by an integral with variable upper limit, such as $$A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$$. | AP problems often ask for $$A'(x)$$, monotonicity, concavity, and interpretation. |
| **Integration by Parts** | A technique derived from the product rule for integrating products. | Frequently tested when substitution does not work directly. |
| **Partial Fraction Decomposition** | Rewriting a rational function into simpler fractions before integrating. | Important for BC symbolic integration, especially with rational expressions. |
| **Improper Integral** | An integral with infinite bounds or an integrand with an infinite discontinuity. | AP exam may ask whether an integral converges or diverges and to justify with limits. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
A[Start with function or rate] --> B{What is being asked?}
B -->|Approximate accumulation| C[Use Riemann sum]
B -->|Exact accumulated change or area| D[Set up definite integral]
B -->|Find family of original functions| E[Find antiderivative]
B -->|Differentiate accumulation function| F[Apply FTC Part 1]

C --> G[Interpret left, right, midpoint, or trapezoidal behavior]
D --> H{Can it be evaluated directly?}
H -->|Yes| I[Use antiderivative and FTC Part 2]
H -->|No| J{Choose technique}
J -->|Substitution works| K[Use substitution]
J -->|Product form| L[Use integration by parts]
J -->|Rational function| M[Use partial fractions]

D --> N{Improper?}
N -->|Yes| O[Rewrite as limit]
O --> P[Test convergence or divergence]
N -->|No| I
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Formula** | **Statement** |
|---|---|
| **Definite Integral as Limit** | $$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\Delta x$$ |
| **Left / Right Riemann Sum Setup** | $$\Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n}$$, with left endpoints $$x_{i-1}=a+(i-1)\Delta x$$ and right endpoints $$x_i=a+i\Delta x$$ |
| **Antiderivative Definition** | If $$F'(x)=f(x)$$, then $$\int f(x)\,dx=F(x)+C$$ |
| **FTC Part 1** | If $$g(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$$, then $$g'(x)=f(x)$$, assuming $$f$$ is continuous |
| **FTC Part 2** | $$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)$$ where $$F'(x)=f(x)$$ |
| **Net Change Theorem** | $$\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)$$ |
| **Change of Variable** | If $$u=g(x)$$, then $$\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx=\int f(u)\,du$$ |
| **Integration by Parts** | $$\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$$ |
| **Partial Fractions, Distinct Linear Factors** | $$\frac{P(x)}{(x-a)(x-b)}=\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x-b}$$ |
| **Improper Integral with Infinite Limit** | $$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx=\lim_{b\to\infty}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$$ |
| **Improper Integral with Discontinuity** | $$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\lim_{c\to a^+}\int_c^b f(x)\,dx$$ or split at the discontinuity |
| **Basic Log Integral** | $$\int \frac{1}{x}\,dx=\ln|x|+C$$ |
| **Exponential / Trig Antiderivatives** | $$\int e^x\,dx=e^x+C,\quad \int \sin x\,dx=-\cos x+C,\quad \int \cos x\,dx=\sin x+C$$ |

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection / Difference** | **AP Significance** |
|---|---|---|
| **Riemann Sum vs. Definite Integral** | A Riemann sum is a finite approximation; the definite integral is the exact limit. | Students must distinguish **approximation** from **exact value**. |
| **Antiderivative vs. Definite Integral** | An antiderivative gives a family of functions; a definite integral gives a number representing net accumulation. | AP often asks you to move between indefinite and definite integration correctly. |
| **FTC Part 1 vs. FTC Part 2** | Part 1 differentiates an accumulation function; Part 2 evaluates a definite integral using antiderivatives. | A major exam trap is using the wrong part of the theorem. |
| **Convergent vs. Divergent Improper Integral** | A convergent improper integral approaches a finite value; a divergent one does not. | You must justify with a **limit**, not just intuition from the graph. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
A[Riemann Sum] --> B[Definite Integral]
B --> C[Accumulation / Net Change]
C --> D[FTC Part 1]
B --> E[FTC Part 2]
E --> F[Antiderivative Evaluation]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **net signed area** with **total area**. If a graph crosses the axis, $$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$$ may be smaller than the actual geometric area.
- Forgetting that **FTC Part 1** gives the integrand evaluated at the variable bound, and requiring the **chain rule** if the upper limit is not just $$x$$, such as $$\frac{d}{dx}\int_1^{x^2} f(t)\,dt=f(x^2)\cdot 2x$$.
- Omitting the constant of integration in **indefinite integrals**.
- Using **partial fractions** before checking whether the rational expression is **proper**. If the degree of the numerator is at least the degree of the denominator, do polynomial division first.
- Declaring an **improper integral** convergent or divergent without rewriting it as a **limit**.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can explain how a **Riemann sum** approximates a definite integral and set one up from a formula or context.
- [ ] I can interpret $$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$$ as **net change** or **net signed area**.
- [ ] I can find and use **antiderivatives** for common functions.
- [ ] I can apply **FTC Part 1** to differentiate accumulation functions, including variable bounds.
- [ ] I can apply **FTC Part 2** to evaluate definite integrals exactly.
- [ ] I can decide when to use **substitution**, **integration by parts**, or **partial fractions**.
- [ ] I can decompose a rational function into **partial fractions** and integrate the result.
- [ ] I can evaluate or test the convergence of an **improper integral** using limits.

# Unit 7: Differential Equations

## Overview
In this unit, you learn how to **model change** when a rate depends on the current state of a system. The AP Calculus BC exam often tests your ability to interpret and solve **differential equations** using **separation of variables**, **slope fields**, **Euler’s method**, and **logistic growth models**.

These topics connect graphical, numerical, and analytical perspectives, so you must be able to move among equations, tables, and visual representations of solutions.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Differential equation** | An equation involving a function and its derivative, such as $$\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$$ | AP questions ask you to interpret what the derivative says about behavior and sometimes solve or approximate solutions |
| **Initial condition** | A given value like $$y(x_0)=y_0$$ that selects one specific solution | Used to find the particular solution rather than a whole family of solutions |
| **Separation of variables** | A method for solving equations that can be rewritten in the form $$\frac{1}{g(y)}\,dy=f(x)\,dx$$ | A core symbolic skill for solving differential equations exactly |
| **Slope field** | A graph showing small line segments with slope determined by $$\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$$ | AP often asks you to sketch solution curves or identify where solutions increase, decrease, or level off |
| **Euler’s method** | A numerical method that uses tangent line steps to approximate a solution | Frequently tested in free-response and multiple-choice as a table-based approximation method |
| **Logistic differential equation** | A growth model of the form $$\frac{dP}{dt}=kP\left(1-\frac{P}{L}\right)$$ | Important because it models limited growth and includes equilibrium behavior |
| **Equilibrium solution** | A constant solution where $$\frac{dy}{dx}=0$$ | Useful for analyzing long-term behavior and logistic models |
| **General vs. particular solution** | General solutions contain constants; particular solutions satisfy initial conditions | AP expects both symbolic solving and using conditions to determine constants |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Given differential equation"] --> B["Identify type of task"]
    B --> C["Solve analytically if separable"]
    B --> D["Approximate numerically with Euler's method"]
    B --> E["Analyze graphically with slope field"]

    C --> F["Separate variables"]
    F --> G["Integrate both sides"]
    G --> H["Solve for constant using initial condition"]
    H --> I["Write particular solution"]

    D --> J["Use $$y_{n+1}=y_n+f(x_n,y_n)\Delta x$$"]
    J --> K["Step forward from initial point"]
    K --> L["Estimate solution value"]

    E --> M["Read slopes from $$\\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$$"]
    M --> N["Determine increasing/decreasing behavior"]
    N --> O["Sketch solution curve through initial point"]

    I --> P["Interpret solution behavior"]
    L --> P
    O --> P
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Formula** | **Meaning / Use** |
|---|---|
| $$\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)$$ | General form of a first-order differential equation |
| $$y(x_0)=y_0$$ | **Initial condition** used to find a particular solution |
| $$\frac{dy}{dx}=g(x)h(y)$$ | A differential equation that may be **separable** |
| $$\frac{1}{h(y)}\,dy=g(x)\,dx$$ | Separated form before integrating |
| $$\int \frac{1}{h(y)}\,dy=\int g(x)\,dx + C$$ | Main integration step for separation of variables |
| $$y_{n+1}=y_n+\frac{dy}{dx}\Delta x=y_n+f(x_n,y_n)\Delta x$$ | **Euler’s method** update formula |
| $$\frac{dP}{dt}=kP$$ | **Exponential growth/decay** model with unrestricted growth |
| $$\frac{dP}{dt}=kP\left(1-\frac{P}{L}\right)$$ | **Logistic growth** model with carrying capacity $$L$$ |
| $$\frac{dP}{dt}=0$$ | Condition for **equilibrium solutions** |
| For logistic growth, equilibria occur at $$P=0$$ and $$P=L$$ | These values make the growth rate zero |

### Important interpretations
- If $$\frac{dy}{dx}>0$$, the solution is **increasing**.
- If $$\frac{dy}{dx}<0$$, the solution is **decreasing**.
- If $$\frac{dy}{dx}=0$$, the solution has a **horizontal tangent** or may be an **equilibrium**.
- In a logistic model:
  - if $$0<P<L$$, then typically $$\frac{dP}{dt}>0$$, so population grows.
  - if $$P>L$$, then typically $$\frac{dP}{dt}<0$$, so population decreases toward $$L$$.

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **How They’re Related** | **Key Difference** |
|---|---|---|
| **Slope field** vs. **Euler’s method** | Both use the derivative $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ to describe local behavior | A **slope field** is graphical; **Euler’s method** gives numerical approximations |
| **General solution** vs. **Particular solution** | Both satisfy the differential equation | A **general solution** contains an arbitrary constant; a **particular solution** uses an initial condition |
| **Exponential model** vs. **Logistic model** | Both model growth with differential equations | Exponential growth uses $$\frac{dP}{dt}=kP$$ and has no limiting capacity; logistic growth includes carrying capacity $$L$$ |
| **Exact solution** vs. **Numerical approximation** | Both estimate the behavior of a function solving the differential equation | An **exact solution** is found algebraically; a **numerical approximation** is used when exact solving is difficult or not required |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Exponential model: $$\\frac{dP}{dt}=kP$$"] --> B["Growth rate proportional to population"]
    C["Logistic model: $$\\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(1-\\frac{P}{L})$$"] --> B
    A --> D["No carrying capacity"]
    C --> E["Carrying capacity $$L$$ limits growth"]
    E --> F["Equilibria at $$P=0$$ and $$P=L$$"]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing **$$\frac{dy}{dx}$$** with **$$y$$** itself. A positive derivative means the function is increasing, not necessarily that the function value is positive.
- Forgetting to use the **initial condition** after integrating a separable equation.
- Making arithmetic errors in **Euler’s method**, especially by using the wrong slope or wrong step size $$\Delta x$$.
- Misreading a **slope field**: the solution curve must follow the short slope segments and pass through the given initial point.
- Treating the logistic model like exponential growth and ignoring the role of **carrying capacity** $$L$$ and equilibrium values.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can identify whether a differential equation is **separable**.
- [ ] I can solve a separable differential equation by separating variables and integrating both sides.
- [ ] I can use an **initial condition** to find a particular solution.
- [ ] I can interpret a **slope field** to determine where solutions increase, decrease, or flatten out.
- [ ] I can sketch or identify a solution curve that matches a given slope field and initial condition.
- [ ] I can apply **Euler’s method** using $$y_{n+1}=y_n+f(x_n,y_n)\Delta x$$.
- [ ] I can distinguish between **exponential** and **logistic** growth models.
- [ ] I can identify and interpret **equilibrium solutions** and long-term behavior in a logistic model.

# Unit 8: Applications of Integration

## Overview
This unit focuses on how definite integrals model accumulated quantities in geometry and motion. In **AP Calculus BC**, you must be able to set up and evaluate integrals for **area between curves**, **volumes of solids**, **arc length**, and **position/velocity/acceleration relationships**, often choosing the correct method from context.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Area between curves** | Using definite integrals to find the region enclosed by two graphs. | AP questions often test whether you choose **top minus bottom** or **right minus left** correctly and split at intersection points when needed. |
| **Integrating with respect to $$x$$ or $$y$$** | Choosing the variable of integration based on the shapes and boundaries of the region. | A major AP skill is recognizing when horizontal slices are easier than vertical slices. |
| **Volume by cross sections** | Finding volume when the cross-sectional area is known as a function of position. | Tests your ability to write $$V = \int A(x)\,dx$$ or $$V = \int A(y)\,dy$$ from geometry. |
| **Disk and washer method** | Volumes of revolution found from circular cross sections perpendicular to the axis of rotation. | AP problems frequently require identifying **outer radius** and **inner radius** correctly. |
| **Shell method** | Volumes of revolution found from cylindrical shells parallel to the axis of rotation. | Important when disk/washer setup is difficult or impossible with the chosen variable. |
| **Arc length** | Measuring the length of a smooth curve using an integral. | Often appears as a setup question; students must know the correct formula and variable. |
| **Motion along a line** | Connecting position, velocity, acceleration, displacement, and total distance. | AP exam questions often distinguish **displacement** from **total distance traveled**. |
| **Accumulation models** | Using integrals to represent total change from a rate. | This is a unifying idea behind all applications and appears throughout FRQs and MCQs. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Identify the quantity asked for] --> B[Sketch region or motion situation]
    B --> C[Choose variable of integration]
    C --> D[Determine bounds of integration]
    D --> E[Select appropriate model]
    E --> E1["Area: top-bottom or right-left"]
    E --> E2["Volume: cross sections, washer, disk, or shell"]
    E --> E3["Arc length: derivative-based formula"]
    E --> E4["Motion: integrate rate functions"]
    E1 --> F[Write the integral carefully]
    E2 --> F
    E3 --> F
    E4 --> F
    F --> G[Evaluate and interpret units/context]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Topic** | **Essential Formula / Rule** |
|---|---|
| **Area between curves, vertical slices** | $$A = \int_a^b \left[f(x) - g(x)\right]\,dx$$ where $$f(x) \ge g(x)$$ |
| **Area between curves, horizontal slices** | $$A = \int_c^d \left[f(y) - g(y)\right]\,dy$$ where the integrand is **right minus left** |
| **Volume from known cross-sectional area** | $$V = \int_a^b A(x)\,dx$$ |
| **Disk method** | $$V = \pi \int_a^b \left[R(x)\right]^2\,dx$$ |
| **Washer method** | $$V = \pi \int_a^b \left(\left[R(x)\right]^2 - \left[r(x)\right]^2\right)\,dx$$ |
| **Shell method** | $$V = 2\pi \int_a^b \left[\text{radius}\right]\left[\text{height}\right]\,dx$$ or $$V = 2\pi \int_c^d \left[\text{radius}\right]\left[\text{height}\right]\,dy$$ |
| **Arc length with respect to $$x$$** | $$L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + \left(f'(x)\right)^2}\,dx$$ |
| **Arc length with respect to $$y$$** | $$L = \int_c^d \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)^2}\,dy$$ |
| **Velocity and position** | If $$v(t) = s'(t)$$, then $$s(b) - s(a) = \int_a^b v(t)\,dt$$ |
| **Acceleration and velocity** | If $$a(t) = v'(t)$$, then $$v(b) - v(a) = \int_a^b a(t)\,dt$$ |
| **Displacement** | $$\text{displacement} = \int_a^b v(t)\,dt$$ |
| **Total distance traveled** | $$\text{total distance} = \int_a^b \left|v(t)\right|\,dt$$ |
| **Average value of a function** | $$f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$$ |

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection** | **Key Difference** | **AP Tip** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Area vs. Volume** | Both use definite integrals to accumulate slices. | **Area** accumulates lengths; **volume** accumulates areas. | Check units: square units for area, cubic units for volume. |
| **Washer/Disk vs. Shell** | Both find volumes of revolution. | **Washer/disk** uses slices perpendicular to axis; **shell** uses slices parallel to axis. | If one setup becomes messy, try the other method. |
| **Displacement vs. Total Distance** | Both come from velocity. | **Displacement** includes sign; **distance** adds absolute movement. | Find where $$v(t) = 0$$ before computing total distance. |
| **Integrating in $$x$$ vs. Integrating in $$y$$** | Both describe the same region or solid. | The expressions and bounds change depending on slice orientation. | Choose the variable that avoids splitting the region when possible. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Region or solid] --> B["Vertical slices (dx)"]
    A --> C["Horizontal slices (dy)"]
    B --> D[Top-bottom expressions]
    B --> E["Disk/washer if revolving around horizontal axis"]
    B --> F["Shell if revolving around vertical axis"]
    C --> G[Right-left expressions]
    C --> H["Disk/washer if revolving around vertical axis"]
    C --> I["Shell if revolving around horizontal axis"]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **area between curves** with **net signed area**. If one curve crosses another, you may need to **split the integral**.
- Using **top minus bottom** when integrating with respect to $$y$$. For horizontal slices, use **right minus left**.
- Forgetting to square both radii in the **washer method**:  
  $$V = \pi \int \left(R^2 - r^2\right)\,d(\text{variable})$$
- Mixing up **displacement** and **total distance traveled**. Total distance requires  
  $$\int \left|v(t)\right|\,dt$$ or splitting where $$v(t)$$ changes sign.
- Using the wrong radius in revolution problems because the axis of rotation is not the coordinate axis. Distances must be measured **from the axis of rotation**, not automatically from the origin.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] I can set up and evaluate an integral for the **area between two curves**.
- [ ] I can decide whether to integrate with respect to $$x$$ or $$y$$ based on the region.
- [ ] I can write a **cross-sectional area** function and integrate it to find volume.
- [ ] I can distinguish and correctly apply the **disk**, **washer**, and **shell** methods.
- [ ] I can identify **radius**, **height**, and bounds correctly for solids of revolution.
- [ ] I can write and evaluate an **arc length** integral from a function or derivative.
- [ ] I can use integrals to relate **position**, **velocity**, and **acceleration**.
- [ ] I can explain the difference between **displacement** and **total distance traveled** and compute both.

When cross sections perpendicular to the axis of revolution are circular, volume is found using $$\pi\int_a^b \big(R(x)\big)^2\,dx$$ for no hole or $$\pi\int_a^b \left(\big(R(x)\big)^2-\big(r(x)\big)^2\right)dx$$ when there is an inner radius.

# Unit 9: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions

## Overview
In this unit, you study curves described in **non-Cartesian ways**: by **parametric equations**, **polar equations**, and **vector-valued functions**. You learn how to differentiate and integrate these representations to find **slope**, **speed**, **arc length**, and **area**, all of which are common AP Calculus BC exam targets in both multiple-choice and free-response questions.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Parametric equations** | A curve described by $$x=f(t), \; y=g(t)$$ using a parameter $$t$$ | AP questions often ask for slope, concavity, motion interpretation, or area using parameter-based formulas |
| **Derivative of a parametric curve** | The slope $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ found by dividing derivatives with respect to $$t$$ | Essential for tangent lines, horizontal/vertical tangents, and critical point analysis |
| **Second derivative for parametrics** | The concavity of a parametric curve found from differentiating $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ with respect to $$t$$ and dividing by $$\frac{dx}{dt}$$ | Frequently tested when analyzing curve shape |
| **Vector-valued functions** | Position given by $$\mathbf{r}(t)=\langle x(t),y(t)\rangle$$ or $$\langle x(t),y(t),z(t)\rangle$$ | Connects calculus to motion: position, velocity, acceleration, and speed |
| **Motion along a curve** | Using $$\mathbf{v}(t)=\mathbf{r}'(t)$$ and $$\mathbf{a}(t)=\mathbf{r}''(t)$$ | AP often frames vector problems as particles moving in the plane |
| **Polar coordinates** | A point given by $$\left(r,\theta\right)$$ where $$x=r\cos\theta,\; y=r\sin\theta$$ | Students must connect polar and rectangular forms and interpret graph behavior |
| **Area in polar form** | Region area found using an integral in terms of $$r$$ and $$\theta$$ | A standard BC application problem, especially with roses, limacons, and loops |
| **Arc length** | Length of a curve in parametric or polar form | Often appears in FRQs requiring setup and sometimes evaluation |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Given a curve: parametric, polar, or vector form"] --> B["Identify the representation"]
    B --> C["Find needed derivatives with respect to the parameter or angle"]
    C --> D["Convert to the requested quantity"]
    D --> E["Slope: use dy/dx"]
    D --> F["Motion: use velocity, acceleration, speed"]
    D --> G["Area: set up definite integral"]
    D --> H["Arc length: apply length formula"]
    E --> I["Analyze tangent lines or concavity"]
    F --> J["Interpret particle motion"]
    G --> K["Evaluate enclosed region"]
    H --> L["Measure curve length"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Topic** | **Formula / Rule** |
|---|---|
| **Parametric derivative** | $$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\frac{dy}{dt}}{\frac{dx}{dt}}, \quad \frac{dx}{dt}\ne 0$$ |
| **Second derivative for parametrics** | $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}$$ |
| **Horizontal tangent** | $$\frac{dy}{dt}=0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{dx}{dt}\ne 0$$ |
| **Vertical tangent** | $$\frac{dx}{dt}=0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{dy}{dt}\ne 0$$ |
| **Area under a parametric curve** | $$A=\int y\,dx=\int_a^b y(t)\,x'(t)\,dt$$ |
| **Vector-valued position** | $$\mathbf{r}(t)=\langle x(t),y(t)\rangle \quad \text{or} \quad \langle x(t),y(t),z(t)\rangle$$ |
| **Velocity** | $$\mathbf{v}(t)=\mathbf{r}'(t)$$ |
| **Acceleration** | $$\mathbf{a}(t)=\mathbf{r}''(t)$$ |
| **Speed** | $$\|\mathbf{v}(t)\|=\sqrt{\left(x'(t)\right)^2+\left(y'(t)\right)^2}$$ |
| **Arc length of a parametric curve** | $$L=\int_a^b \sqrt{\left(x'(t)\right)^2+\left(y'(t)\right)^2}\,dt$$ |
| **Polar to rectangular** | $$x=r\cos\theta,\quad y=r\sin\theta$$ |
| **Rectangular to polar** | $$r^2=x^2+y^2,\quad \tan\theta=\frac{y}{x}$$ |
| **Slope for a polar curve** | $$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta+r\cos\theta}{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta-r\sin\theta}$$ |
| **Area of a polar region** | $$A=\frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta \left(r(\theta)\right)^2\,d\theta$$ |
| **Arc length of a polar curve** | $$L=\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\left(r(\theta)\right)^2+\left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta$$ |

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **Connection** | **Key Difference** | **AP Use** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Parametric equations** vs. **vector-valued functions** | Both describe motion or curves using a parameter | Parametric form emphasizes coordinates separately; vector form packages them into $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ | AP may switch notation but expects the same derivative ideas |
| **Velocity** vs. **speed** | Both come from position over time | **Velocity** is a vector; **speed** is its magnitude | Students often compute velocity when the question asks for speed |
| **Polar area** vs. **parametric area** | Both use definite integrals to measure regions | Polar area uses $$\frac{1}{2}\int r^2\,d\theta$$; parametric area uses $$\int y\,dx$$ | Choosing the correct formula is a common exam skill |
| **First derivative** vs. **second derivative** in parametrics | Both require chain rule ideas | First derivative gives slope; second derivative gives concavity | AP often asks for both on the same curve-analysis problem |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Parametric: x(t), y(t)"] --> B["dy/dx from derivatives in t"]
    C["Polar: r(theta)"] --> D["Convert using x=r cos theta, y=r sin theta or use polar slope formula"]
    E["Vector: r(t)"] --> F["Differentiate to get velocity and acceleration"]
    B --> G["Curve analysis"]
    D --> G
    F --> H["Motion analysis"]
```

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **$$\frac{dy}{dt}$$** with **$$\frac{dy}{dx}$$**. For parametric curves, slope requires dividing by **$$\frac{dx}{dt}$$**.
- Forgetting the conditions for **horizontal** and **vertical tangents**. A zero numerator or denominator alone is not enough; check the other derivative is nonzero.
- Using the wrong interval for **polar area**, especially when the graph traces the same region more than once.
- Forgetting that **speed** is the magnitude of velocity, so it must be nonnegative:
  $$\|\mathbf{v}(t)\| \neq \mathbf{v}(t).$$
- Missing the extra chain-rule step in the **second derivative** for parametric equations:
  $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \neq \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right).$$

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] I can compute **$$\frac{dy}{dx}$$** for a curve given by $$x(t)$$ and $$y(t)$$.
- [ ] I can determine where a parametric curve has **horizontal** or **vertical tangents**.
- [ ] I can find **$$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$** for a parametric curve and use it to analyze **concavity**.
- [ ] I can interpret **position**, **velocity**, **acceleration**, and **speed** for a **vector-valued function**.
- [ ] I can convert between **polar** and **rectangular** coordinates using $$x=r\cos\theta$$ and $$y=r\sin\theta$$.
- [ ] I can set up and evaluate **polar area** using $$A=\frac{1}{2}\int r^2\,d\theta$$.
- [ ] I can set up **arc length** integrals for both **parametric** and **polar** curves.
- [ ] I can decide which formula fits a problem based on whether the curve is given in **parametric**, **polar**, or **vector** form.

# Unit 10: Infinite Sequences and Series

## Overview
This unit develops the tools for deciding whether **infinite sequences** and **infinite series** converge, and for representing functions with **power series**, **Taylor series**, and **Maclaurin series**. On the AP Calculus BC exam, these topics appear in both conceptual and computational forms, especially when choosing the correct **convergence test**, finding **intervals of convergence**, and estimating error.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept** | **What It Is** | **Why It Matters (AP angle)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Sequence convergence** | Determines whether the terms $$a_n$$ approach a finite limit as $$n \to \infty$$ | Often the first step in understanding whether a related series can converge |
| **Series and partial sums** | A series $$\sum a_n$$ is the sum of infinitely many terms, analyzed through partial sums $$S_n$$ | AP questions often ask whether a series converges, diverges, or converges conditionally/absolutely |
| **Geometric series** | A series of the form $$\sum ar^n$$ or $$\sum ar^{n-1}$$ with convergence based on $$|r|<1$$ | One of the fastest recognition-based topics on the exam |
| **Convergence tests** | Methods such as the **nth-term test**, **integral test**, **comparison tests**, **ratio test**, and **alternating series test** | A major AP skill is selecting and justifying the correct test |
| **Absolute vs. conditional convergence** | **Absolute convergence** means $$\sum |a_n|$$ converges; **conditional convergence** means $$\sum a_n$$ converges but $$\sum |a_n|$$ diverges | Frequently tested in free-response explanations |
| **Power series** | A series of the form $$\sum c_n(x-a)^n$$ centered at $$x=a$$ | Used to find **radius** and **interval of convergence** |
| **Taylor and Maclaurin series** | Polynomial-like infinite expansions that represent functions near a center | AP BC regularly asks students to build, recognize, or use these series |
| **Error bounds** | Estimates for how close a partial sum is to the true value | Important when approximating functions and justifying accuracy |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Identify the expression] --> B{Sequence or series?}
    B -->|Sequence $$a_n$$| C[Find $$\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n$$]
    C --> D[Decide whether the sequence converges]
    B -->|Series $$\sum a_n$$| E[Check the nth-term test]
    E --> F{Does $$\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n \neq 0$$ or fail to exist?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Series diverges]
    F -->|No| H[Choose a convergence test]
    H --> I["Geometric / p-series / telescoping?"]
    H --> J[Comparison or limit comparison]
    H --> K[Integral test]
    H --> L[Ratio or root test]
    H --> M[Alternating series test]
    I --> N[Determine convergence or divergence]
    J --> N
    K --> N
    L --> N
    M --> N
    N --> O{If it converges, absolutely or conditionally?}
    O --> P[Check $$\sum |a_n|$$]
    P --> Q[State conclusion with justification]
    Q --> R["If power series: find radius and interval of convergence"]
    R --> S["If approximation: apply error bound"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Rule / Formula** | **Statement** |
|---|---|
| **Sequence convergence** | A sequence converges if $$\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = L$$ for some finite $$L$$ |
| **nth-term test for divergence** | If $$\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n \neq 0$$ or does not exist, then $$\sum a_n$$ **diverges** |
| **Geometric series** | $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} ar^n$$ converges if $$|r|<1$$ and then $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} ar^n=\frac{a}{1-r}$$ |
| **p-series** | $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^p}$$ converges if $$p>1$$ and diverges if $$p\le 1$$ |
| **Integral test** | If $$a_n=f(n)$$ where $$f$$ is positive, continuous, and decreasing, then $$\sum a_n$$ and $$\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx$$ either both converge or both diverge |
| **Direct comparison test** | Compare $$0\le a_n\le b_n$$ with a known series to conclude convergence or divergence |
| **Limit comparison test** | If $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{b_n}=c$$ where $$0<c<\infty$$, then $$\sum a_n$$ and $$\sum b_n$$ behave the same |
| **Alternating series test** | $$\sum (-1)^n b_n$$ or $$\sum (-1)^{n-1} b_n$$ converges if $$b_n>0$$, $$b_{n+1}\le b_n$$, and $$\lim_{n\to\infty} b_n=0$$ |
| **Alternating series error bound** | For an alternating series satisfying the test, $$|S-S_n|\le b_{n+1}$$ |
| **Absolute convergence** | If $$\sum |a_n|$$ converges, then $$\sum a_n$$ converges absolutely |
| **Ratio test** | Let $$L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|$$. If $$L<1$$, the series converges absolutely; if $$L>1$$ or $$L=\infty$$, it diverges; if $$L=1$$, the test is inconclusive |
| **Power series** | $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n(x-a)^n$$ has a **radius of convergence** $$R$$ and converges for $$|x-a|<R$$ |
| **Taylor series** | $$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n$$ |
| **Maclaurin series** | A Taylor series centered at $$a=0$$: $$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}x^n$$ |
| **Lagrange remainder** | $$|R_n(x)|\le \frac{M|x-a|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}$$, where $$M$$ bounds $$|f^{(n+1)}(t)|$$ on the interval |

### Must-know common Maclaurin series
- $$\displaystyle \frac{1}{1-x}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x^n,\quad |x|<1$$
- $$\displaystyle e^x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n!}$$
- $$\displaystyle \sin x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}$$
- $$\displaystyle \cos x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$$
- $$\displaystyle \ln(1+x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}\frac{x^n}{n},\quad -1<x\le 1$$
- $$\displaystyle \arctan x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{2n+1},\quad -1\le x\le 1$$

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept Pair** | **How They Are Related** | **Key Difference** |
|---|---|---|
| **Sequence vs. Series** | A series $$\sum a_n$$ is built from the terms of a sequence $$a_n$$ | A sequence studies terms; a series studies sums of terms |
| **Absolute vs. Conditional Convergence** | Both describe convergent series | Absolute convergence requires $$\sum |a_n|$$ to converge; conditional does not |
| **Taylor polynomial vs. Taylor series** | Both approximate a function near $$x=a$$ using derivatives | A polynomial has finitely many terms; a series has infinitely many |
| **Radius vs. Interval of Convergence** | Both describe where a power series converges | Radius is a distance $$R$$ from the center; interval includes endpoint testing |

## Common AP Exam Traps
- Confusing the **nth-term test**: if $$\lim a_n=0$$, that does **not** prove the series converges.
- Forgetting to test the **endpoints** after finding the radius of convergence for a power series.
- Using the **alternating series test** to claim **absolute convergence**; it only proves convergence, not absolute convergence.
- Applying the **ratio test** and stopping when $$L=1$$; this result is **inconclusive**.
- Mixing up a **Taylor polynomial approximation** with the full **Taylor series**, or forgetting the center $$a$$.

## Quick Review Checklist
- [ ] I can determine whether a **sequence** $$a_n$$ converges and find its limit.
- [ ] I can identify and evaluate a **geometric series** and recognize a **p-series**.
- [ ] I can choose an appropriate **convergence test** and justify my reasoning.
- [ ] I can distinguish between **divergence**, **absolute convergence**, and **conditional convergence**.
- [ ] I can find the **radius** and **interval of convergence** of a **power series**, including endpoint testing.
- [ ] I can write or use **Taylor** and **Maclaurin series** for common functions.
- [ ] I can form a **Taylor polynomial** of a given degree centered at $$a$$.
- [ ] I can estimate approximation error using the **alternating series error bound** or **Lagrange remainder**.
